title: PackClient
subtitle: Reverse Engineering a Modular RAT Framework
author: Ivan Immanuel Shaji

sections.title: From Launcher to recovered Core
sections.deck: The recovered chain connects the signed host, injected Launcher, PLK1 delivery, Core behavior, persistence, and historical C2 traffic.

blocks.text:
This research follows one PackClient build from its signed host and sideloaded carrier into a suspended 32-bit surrogate, the injected Donut package, Launcher delivery, and the recovered Core.

| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| Launcher | Recovered framing, authentication, PLK1/cache, active-session, and `1RCP` contracts |
| Core | Reconstructed a 985,088-byte `PackClientCore.dll` directly from historical PLK1 traffic and mapped its exports, configuration, plugin interfaces, commands, and screenshot producer |
| Historical traffic | Reassembled `PLH1 -> PLC1 -> PLA1 -> PLK1`, followed by bidirectional Core traffic and 15 `PV10` JPEG frames |
| Persistence | Distinguished the normal full-EXE path from the broken task produced when a sandbox invoked the carrier DLL directly through `rundll32.exe` |

The Launcher's raw-BGRX `1RCP` worker and the Core's GDI/WIC `PV10` producer are separate recovered paths. No component linking them was found, and no plugin binary was present in the available traffic, memory, or cache material. [PackClient Core](references/core-analysis.html), [Evidence](references/evidence.html)

sections.title: From a signed host to the embedded launcher
sections.deck: The staged helper explains the sideload. The embedded package reveals the Donut loader, mapper, Launcher, and delivered Core.

blocks.text:
The July 2026 Tax Notice lineage stages a signed NV Access/NVDA executable beside a malicious `nvdaHelperRemote.dll`. The host imports that helper by bare filename, allowing the colocated carrier to satisfy the import. Its import table contains only `ExitProcess` and `injection_initialize`; host RVA `0x1004` calls the helper through IAT slot `0xF268`. The legitimate helper name is documented by NV Access. [Artifact identity and lineage](references/evidence.html), [NVDA helper documentation](https://github.com/nvaccess/nvda/blob/master/nvdaHelper/readme.md)

The injected call-over-data package contains a Donut instance and embedded executable A. Four-byte terminal glue recovers the instance pointer from the opening `CALL`; the following 11,647 bytes exactly match Donut `LOADER_EXE_X86` at commit `47758d787209dd1744f58c140102ac91b649df16`, followed by 23 zero bytes. Donut maps A, and A maps `PackClientLauncher.exe` B. [Transformed record and loader](references/architecture.html)

Triage repeatedly records remote package writes into a newly created suspended 32-bit `svchost.exe`, followed by `SetThreadContext` on its primary thread. Across twelve July/August tasks, the complete 417,792-byte protected allocation is stable at SHA-256 `E49581067CC2AA5ABD09C8DF42D6FBD87CB064A9363FE8B52D8369FD1C51FFE5`. It contains the separately reconstructed 415,071-byte logical record; the extra 2,721 allocation bytes remain unexplained and the two identities must not be collapsed. One exemplar records 53 write-labelled events into PID 844 at `0x00440000`, followed by `SetThreadContext` on primary thread 4600. This supports thread execution hijacking (`T1055.003`), not classic process hollowing or remote-thread injection. The carrier's exact static write API/call site and installed instruction-pointer value remain unresolved. [Carrier and A-to-B mapping](references/architecture.html)

The Launcher implements transport, PLK1 delivery and caching, active-session handoff, and an early screenshot-worker mode. Historical traffic supplies the Core that follows PLK1 and the commands and `PV10` frames exchanged after it starts.

| Object | Recorded size | Identity anchor |
|---|---:|---|
| Tax Notice host | 120,984 bytes | SHA-256 begins `93DD8B7B393289F8` |
| Sideload carrier | 455,527 bytes | SHA-256 begins `7295090C2CB63EBC` |
| Reconstructed Launcher B | 271,872-byte PE32 executable | SHA-256 begins `46B34789196733FA` |
| Recovered Core | 985,088-byte PE32 DLL | SHA-256 begins `4DE6EF8647FB4B59` |

Complete hashes appear in the [identity index](evidence.html#identities).

sections.title: The 1RCP screenshot boundary
sections.deck: The worker implements a small, exact protocol. The endpoint creator and downstream consumer remain unidentified.

blocks.text:
The worker is selected by an early argument-dispatch branch, before the later active-session/Core path. The interface is `/scr_cap_worker <endpoint-utf8> [monitor-index]`. Its body runs in the already launched process and inherits that process’s token, session and environment. The wrapper exits after the worker returns; the later token-based launch path cannot be used to infer the worker’s original security context. [Activation and context](references/screenshot-ipc.html)

The endpoint argument is converted to UTF-16 and passed to `CreateFileW` with read/write access, no sharing and `OPEN_EXISTING`. There is one open attempt. The recovered path contains no endpoint creator, named-pipe server, wait-for-pipe loop or peer authentication. A named pipe is strongly supported by context, but the argument’s namespace is not recovered; the API itself also accepts other paths. [Screenshot IPC reference](references/screenshot-ipc.html)

After the first successful capture, the worker emits READY. It then accumulates exactly 20 command bytes, checks the magic and dispatches the request type. Correct-magic types other than 3 and 5 are ignored. Bad magic, a failed read or a zero-byte read ends the command loop without a protocol reply. The diagram scopes the successful capture paths and command dispatch; it is not a packet capture.

The header is five little-endian DWORDs. The bytes `31 52 43 50` spell `1RCP`; as a DWORD the magic is `0x50435231`.

| Type | Direction | Meaning | Dimensions and payload |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Worker → peer | READY | Captured width and height; payload length zero |
| 3 | Peer → worker | Recapture | Request DWORDs 2–4 are ignored |
| 2 | Worker → peer | Frame response | Width, height and following pixel-byte length |
| 5 | Peer → worker | Exit | Request DWORDs 2–4 are ignored; no reply |

This distinction matters for an independent parser. Zero-filled request fields are a synthetic fixture convention, not a requirement imposed by the worker. The request loop also does not drain extra bytes according to the request’s last DWORD; it reads the next 20-byte header. Worker process exit codes are separate from these message types.

The selected monitor supplies positive width and height. The DIB uses 32-bit `BI_RGB` with a negative height, producing top-down rows. Each pixel is blue, green, red and an unused fourth byte; meaningful alpha is not established. Stride is `width × 4`, with no additional per-row padding. The expected payload is `width × height × 4`; the IA-32 reconstruction found no separate arithmetic overflow guard. The actual response length is taken from the framebuffer vector’s end-minus-begin distance. [Pixel calculation and layout](references/screenshot-ipc.html)

**The verified dataflow ends at `WriteFile` on the supplied endpoint.** Within recovered B, no scoped call/data edge carries those pixels into Winsock, PLK1, the encrypted transport, or a JPEG/PV10 conversion path. An external peer could transform or forward the pixels, but its implementation is missing. The recovered worker interface does not establish end-to-end exfiltration. [External peer boundaries](references/screenshot-ipc.html)

sections.title: Framing, authentication and the missing key writer
sections.deck: The lower transport can be reconstructed more precisely than the available runtime traffic can validate it.

blocks.text:
The outer frame starts with a little-endian word formed by `0x5A400000 | body_length`. The receiver checks `(frame_word >> 22) == 0x169`, bounds the nonzero body at `0x3FFFFF`, reads it exactly, and requires at least four bytes for the type. Thus `24 00 40 5A` means a 36-byte body and a 40-byte total frame. Treating the prefix as an entire message would produce an incorrect decoder. [Framing and handshake](references/protocol-reference.html)

| Offset | Bytes | Outer-frame meaning |
|---:|---:|---|
| `0x00` | 4 | Prefix combined with body length |
| `0x04` | 4 | Little-endian type DWORD, part of the body |
| `0x08` | Variable | Payload; body length minus four |

B sends PLH1 and PLA1 in plaintext type `0x15`. Its first framed receive accepts PLC1 either directly in type `0x15` or through an authenticated outer `0x16` envelope with inner type `0x15`, provided the envelope keys are initialized. This receive precedes Core loading. PLH1 is a 32-byte client hello; PLC1 is the 24-byte server challenge; PLA1 is the 40-byte client authentication object. PLH1 includes version 1, an unresolved word set to `0x20`, fixed fields, a tick count and the process ID. PLC1 contributes a 16-byte challenge at offsets `0x08..0x17`; challenge generation lives in the missing server.

PLA1 uses HMAC-SHA-256 over exactly **42 bytes**. It is not a hash of the entire hello and challenge:

```text
PLH1[0x10:0x20]  // 16 bytes
|| PLC1[0x08:0x18]  // 16 bytes
|| PLH1[0x0C:0x10]  //  4 bytes
|| PLH1[0x06:0x08]  //  2 bytes
|| "PLK1"          //  4 bytes
```

The PSK comes from `PACK_LAUNCH_PSK`; missing or empty values select the 19-byte fallback `pack-launch-dev-psk`. The passive tool only uses that fallback when explicitly requested. After sending PLA1, the recovered function does not check a separate post-authentication acknowledgement. These are build-specific static facts, not observations of a successful live handshake. [Handshake evidence](references/evidence.html)

### Authentication gates encrypted receive

Type `0x16` is an inbound encrypted envelope. In this B image the send path constructs only type `0x15`; symmetric support must not be assumed. The envelope carries a version byte, 16-byte IV, four-byte **big-endian** ciphertext length, ciphertext, and 32-byte HMAC tag. The length field’s byte order differs from the surrounding little-endian framing.

The MAC covers version, IV, encoded length and ciphertext, excluding the outer frame/type and the trailing tag. A tag match gates AES-256-CBC decryption with BCrypt block padding; the resulting plaintext must begin with inner type `0x15`. The recovered tag comparison exits early, so the report does not describe it as constant-time.

A ready byte at B RVA `0x41C44` gates a 32-byte AES key at `0x41C48` and a separate 32-byte HMAC key at `0x41C68`. The completed B census found reads but no initializer, setter or derivation. The handshake PSK/HMAC was not shown to flow into those globals. An unrecovered in-process component could initialize them; absent that state, encrypted receive remains disabled. Envelope-key initialization remains unresolved. [Envelope key origin](references/protocol-reference.html)

sections.title: Delivery is gated by a cache round trip
sections.deck: Freshly received bytes do not pass directly to the PE loader. The cache is part of the acceptance path.

blocks.text: PLK1 validates magic/version, original and transferred size bounds, sequence and chunk-copy state, optional raw LZ4 decompression, and the final plaintext SHA-256. Active callers request slot 0, corresponding to `PackClientCore.primary.dll`. Generic shared support can name a secondary slot, but the bounded caller census found no reachable request for it in this build. [Delivery and Core audit](references/core-and-artifact-audit.html)

For a fresh transfer, `Save` must succeed. `TryLoad` must then decrypt and independently re-hash the stored plaintext. Only that reloaded vector is returned to the PE wrapper and `MemoryLoadLibraryEx`. This exact branch order matters: a decoder that accepts the network object alone models only part of the launcher’s acceptance conditions.

Eight complete historical transfers now validate the network object independently: each uses eleven ordered type-`0x15` chunks, ten of 65,536 bytes and a final 14,357-byte chunk. Their 669,717-byte raw-LZ4 object decompresses to the same 985,088-byte Core and sender-declared SHA-256. The capability resolution and CryptProtect/Unprotect dataflow still strongly support current-user DPAPI protection for the relative cache; the absolute runtime base remains unresolved. [Positive-flow reconstruction](references/protocol-reference.html)

sections.title: The delivered Core is recovered
sections.deck: Historical PLK1 traffic reconstructs the Core and continues into observed commands and screenshot frames.

blocks.text:
All eight complete PLK1 transfers—four in `260715-wd77daas7l` and four in `260716-dhnz7aft6z`—produce one canonical 985,088-byte x86 `PackClientCore.dll`, SHA-256 `4DE6EF8647FB4B599966A233740CB0514D1E71B8019A1A1792ED7E1E514EDF1C`. A separate census found 352 retained memory records from eight Core processes; every record's 753,664-byte `.text` matches SHA-256 `F06FF7AB6D62B761344CAECBCC6857912F7543F43C0E5FF462D2174BADB0CA3F`.

All 11 exports are accounted for, including `Main`, `MainMinimal`, `MainWithConfig`, `RunWithConfig`, `PackClientDll_AbiVersion`, `PackClientDll_Run`, `PackClientDll_TrySystemSessionHandoff`, `PackClient_AllocStoredPluginImageW`, `PackClient_FreeStoredPluginImage`, `ProbeEntry` and `RunDualWithConfig`. `PackClientDll_Run` confirms the Launcher's five-field view: host at `+0x00`, 16-bit port at `+0x04`, group at `+0x08`, optional tag at `+0x0C`, and optional configuration string at `+0x10`. [Core ABI and exports](references/core-and-artifact-audit.html)

The Core resolves a modern plugin ABI—`PackPlugin_GetAbiVersion`, `PackPlugin_GetFeatureId` and `PackPlugin_OnLoad`—and retains a legacy `Main` loader. A pre-dispatch gate requires at least `RunWithConfig` or `Main`; the modern ABI is additional validation, not the sole admissible entry. Eleven canonical feature-to-DLL mappings, screen-codec sidecars, the idempotent `init -> chunk -> commit` raw-LZ4 transaction, legacy LZ4/zlib delivery, activation policy and paired current-user-DPAPI `.pblob`/JSON store were recovered. That plugin store writes through a temporary file, flushes, atomically replaces the cache and records JSON metadata including feature, version, architecture, hash, size and timestamps. It is distinct from the Launcher's SHA-256-addressed Core cache. `store=registry` means Core's internal module registry, not a Windows Registry plugin store. A separate `CLIENTCOREUPD` path writes DPAPI-protected chunks under `HKCU\Software\PackMonitorClient\LauncherDllStore\<bits>\Primary`; WinHTTP is not that update path. No plugin binary, paired cache, completed delivery or update transaction, or activated plugin mapping appears in the available artifacts. The implementation is present, but no plugin delivery or activation was observed.

Historical Core traffic includes plaintext `INP HELLO`, `STARTUP PROBE`/`STARTUP OK`, `KTL OFFLINE` and `PREVIEW ENABLE`/`REQ`/`ACK` exchanges. The recovered implementation and observed traffic line up as follows:

| Surface | Observed traffic | Recovered Core behavior | Remaining boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Session/startup | `INP HELLO`, `STARTUP PROBE` and `STARTUP OK` | Session/control router and startup-probe branch | Live Core exchange; no server implementation |
| Preview | Enable/request/ack exchanges and 15 `PV10` JPEG frames | GDI/WIC capture and `PV10` producer | No bridge to Launcher `1RCP` |
| Keylogger | `KTL OFFLINE` telemetry | Hook, archive, sync and clipboard-telemetry paths | No captured keystroke contents |
| Plugins | No transaction, cache pair or plugin bytes | Staged protocol, ABI, loader and DPAPI cache | Capability only |
| Core update | No transaction | `CLIENTCOREUPD` validation and registry store | Static only; WinHTTP is not attributed to this branch |
| Auth envelope | No type-`0x16` frames | Optional Core KDF and AES-CBC/HMAC envelope | No deployed PSK or encrypted message |
| ETCHOOK | No activation traffic | Regex-controlled clipboard replacement | Static capability only |

The Core's built-in preview producer uses GDI capture and scaling, `GetDIBits`, WIC JPEG encoding and a bytewise `PV10` serializer; fifteen historical type-18 frames agree with that format. This is distinct from the Launcher's raw-BGRX `1RCP` worker, and no recovered component bridges the two. The Core's ETCHOOK path also implements regex-controlled ANSI/Unicode clipboard replacement. Proofpoint previously reported PackClient's clipboard-replacement capability. Analysis of this Core build adds the built-in patterns and concrete control formats.

Core's authenticated type-`0x16` record uses a little-endian ciphertext length. Nonempty local `auth_psk` derives independent keys as `SHA256("PACKAPP|AES256|v1|" || raw_psk)` and `SHA256("PACKAPP|HMAC|v1|" || raw_psk)`; an empty value clears readiness and both keys. Core wraps the entire original type-plus-payload, sets the outer message type to `C + 0x35`, and redispatches the decrypted inner record; original types `0x15` and `0x16` are not wrapped. The Launcher's pre-Core type-`0x16` instead uses a big-endian ciphertext length, unresolved key state, and accepts only a decrypted inner type `0x15`. The same outer message type therefore has a different layout after the connection enters the Core phase. [Core configuration and application envelope](references/core-analysis.html)

sections.title: Staying with the active console session
sections.deck: The launcher contains an active-console relaunch mechanism with a 30-attempt spawn loop. It should not be conflated with the original chain’s elevation step.

blocks.text:
The active-session path resolves a bootstrap executable, preserves a constrained set of special arguments, duplicates the current process token as a primary launch token and assigns it to the target console session before calling `CreateProcessAsUserW`. A separately selected user token can supply the environment; it is not the launch token. This is separate from the early screenshot mode, which exits through its own wrapper. [Token selection](references/active-session-handoff.html), [Spawn contract](references/active-session-handoff.html)

| Parameter or state | Recovered behavior |
|---|---|
| Application and command | Null application-name argument; mutable quoted command line |
| Child environment | Optional Unicode environment; handle inheritance disabled |
| Desktop and visibility | `WinSta0\Default`; hidden/no-window startup |
| Creation flags | `0x09000400`: breakaway, no window, Unicode environment |
| Retry bound | At most 30 attempts; one-second sleep after failure |
| Session-drift polling | 200 ms; a valid different console ID triggers replacement |

On successful drift replacement, the launcher closes child handles and exits the old process. It uses canonical `-acsi` state for this handoff. The recovered API makes the continuity mechanism concrete; it does not establish which elevation API produced the original high-integrity host in the second runtime evidence set. [Session drift](references/active-session-handoff.html)

sections.title: The reconstructed code appears in memory
sections.deck: The first runtime set links static structure, private mappings, a thread start and launcher-specific live state.

blocks.text:
The first runtime capture preserves a bare 32-bit `SysWOW64\svchost.exe`, PID 5812, an NvSvc task, VMMap state, a user-mode dump and a late Process Monitor capture. The runtime correspondence below comes from passive examination of those artifacts.

VMMap’s 408 KiB private executable allocation at `0x002E0000` was an investigative lead. Its displayed “Thread Environment Block” label did not identify its contents. The dump’s package structure, embedded offsets, PE metadata and section hashes supplied that identification. [Memory correspondence](references/evidence.html)

| Object in PID 5812 | Runtime location | Why the match matters |
|---|---|---|
| Protected package allocation | `0x002E0000`; 417,792 bytes | A/B occur at the logical record offsets `0x128D` / `0x1CC1`; this full allocation is distinct from the 415,071-byte decoded record |
| Mapped A | `0x02C70000`; image size `0x64000` | Entry RVA `0x1308`, timestamp `0x6A27AE4B` and PE layout agree |
| Mapped B | `0x05410000`; image size `0x48000` | Entry RVA `0x12FAC`, timestamp `0x6A3CB0B5` and immutable sections agree |
| Thread 1884 | Start `0x02C71308` | Exactly mapped A plus its entry RVA |

The complete protected allocation has SHA-256 `E49581067CC2AA5ABD09C8DF42D6FBD87CB064A9363FE8B52D8369FD1C51FFE5`; the embedded 415,071-byte logical record has SHA-256 `0419AE7381CAA97172C40F5AEA601B8A22F1F58D27F3930509AF5808E043F65E`. The mapped images are outside the registered module list. B-specific state includes the named mutant `PackClientLauncher.Session.9b2126fc5ed31443` under the BaseNamedObjects namespace, effective configuration and formatted launcher diagnostics. This converging evidence supports B’s activity more strongly than a lone Core-related string or a suspicious process name would.

The bounded PE/marker census found no independently identifiable Core image in this local dump. That does not exclude headerless content, missing pages, another moment in the process’s life, or unavailable artifacts. It also does not reveal the instruction-level mechanism that populated this surrogate. [Runtime validation](references/runtime-validation.html)

sections.title: A second runtime set preserves the creation chain
sections.deck: Local captures connect sideloading, elevation and persistence; controlled Triage tasks separate the intended EXE path from a direct-DLL artifact.

blocks.text: During controlled execution in Windows 11, Process Monitor records successful loading of the adjacent helper after two earlier `0xC0000906` failures. A medium-integrity Tax Notice process, PID 5952, relaunches as high-integrity PID 2116. The elevated host creates the bare surrogate and the task-creation branch below. The session includes separate launch attempts; the process relationships are tied to their recorded creation events. [Native process evidence](references/runtime-validation.html)

The relationship is specific: **svchost 3696 and schtasks 4600 are siblings under 2116**. Conhost 8248 belongs below schtasks. The parent exits shortly after creating its children; its continued appearance in a process tree preserves ancestry, not liveness. Later reuse of a numeric PID must be joined to a new process start and lifetime.

Native file and registry records establish installation beneath `C:\ProgramData\NVIDIA Corporation\NvSvc`, hidden/backdated copies and HKCU Run/RunOnce writes in this chain. Task XML and the creation record establish NvSvc persistence. Task Scheduler shows the at-logon trigger, ProgramData action and configured user context. Unlike the first set’s timestamp mismatch alone, the second runtime evidence set includes records of the backdating operation. [Persistence evidence](references/evidence.html)

Controlled Triage tasks close the apparent persistence discrepancy. Full-EXE execution copies and schedules `Tax_Notice_23665.exe`. Direct invocation as `rundll32.exe …nvdahelperremote.dll,#1` bypasses the expected signed host, so the carrier treats the sandbox host as its executable and persists a copied `rundll32.exe` without the DLL argument. That action cannot replay the original entry point. The two process trees therefore represent execution modes and sandbox context, not distinct PackClient variants.

“Highest privileges” here belongs to the selected current user; it does not mean SYSTEM. A later persisted-path launch is observed, but the saved local evidence does not resolve every trigger as logon versus on-demand. In isolation, the bare local surrogate properties support an anomalous launcher host but do not identify an injection subtype. The cross-task Triage record supplies the missing higher-level classification: remote writes followed by `SetThreadContext` on the suspended primary thread support thread execution hijacking (`T1055.003`), while the precise write primitive and installed instruction pointer remain unresolved.

The second dump records a 415,071-byte transformed package and a private B mapping. The recorded comparison reports eight differing bytes at three package sites, plus normalized B correspondence after accounting for relocations and the import address table. **The package/B residence result stands separately from the proposed explanation for those eight bytes.** Three simple 6666-to-443 port substitutions would ordinarily account for six changed bytes, so the exact per-site before/after transcript is still required. The eight-byte result is not a proved port patch. [Recorded comparison and open gap](references/evidence.html)

sections.title: Local failure and historical success are separate
sections.deck: The local captures show failed attempts; the July public captures preserve an established PackClient session.

blocks.text:
PID 5812’s preserved environment and formatted buffers identify `154[.]36[.]188[.]201:443`, a slot-0 pull attempt and `WSA=10060`. The PID 3696 set adds 373 ICMP host-unreachable messages quoting TCP SYNs to the same destination, plus two direct `SYN_SENT` socket views. These local artifacts establish attempts, not a completed session.

The historical July Triage streams answer the missing question: they contain server PLC1, client PLA1, complete PLK1 delivery and post-Core bidirectional application traffic on the same TCP/443 endpoint. The traffic is raw PackClient, not TLS. The September researcher reruns `260908-zwr5naybjb` and `260909-abma8sab28` again reached only the greeting/retry stage because the server returned no application data. [Historical and local network evidence](references/core-and-artifact-audit.html)

| Evidence object | What it establishes | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| PID 5812 dump buffers | Configured attempt and timeout | No successful handshake in that local capture |
| PID 3696 TCP/IP/PCAP views | Failed SYN behavior associated with PID 3696 | Packet file itself has no PID metadata |
| July historical Triage flows | Successful Launcher authentication, PLK1 and Core traffic | Public sandbox scope; no server implementation |
| September researcher reruns | PLH1 retries and server non-response | Does not explain the server-side cause |

Port 443 alone does not establish TLS or HTTPS. Capture dates and execution contexts remain attached to every claim: a historical successful session does not convert the September non-response into success, and the later failure does not negate the July delivered Core. [Evidence boundaries](references/evidence.html)

sections.title: The worker failed before READY
sections.deck: A potentially unsafe lifetime sequence is real static evidence. The available debugger record does not prove it caused the final failure.

blocks.text: The recovered capture path creates a DIB, selects it, calls `BitBlt`, restores the old selection, calls `DeleteObject`, performs DC cleanup and later copies from the saved bits pointer. Microsoft’s API contract explains why a successful deletion would matter: deleting the DIB frees system-owned bits. But `DeleteObject` can fail, and a breakpoint before its call does not capture a successful return. [CreateDIBSection](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-createdibsection), [DeleteObject](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/wingdi/nf-wingdi-deleteobject)

Debugger evidence spans three separate attempts with manual changes. The process IDs and addresses cannot be combined into a controlled before/after experiment.

| PID | Observation | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| 8892 | Source `0x03260000`, copy length `0x510000`; memory-map lookup rejects the source | Successful deletion and an unmodified baseline |
| 8148 | Pre-delete breakpoint; later copy breakpoint uses source `0x02830000` | A breakpoint is not an access violation or a deletion result |
| 8040 | AV at RVA `0xA567`, `push [edi+8]`, `EDI=0x13C`; zero READY bytes received | Correct application of every manual change and the crash’s causal chain |

The copy length `0x510000` equals `1536 × 864 × 4`, consistent with the captured monitor geometry. Arithmetic agreement does not establish buffer lifetime or ownership. [Attempt-level validation](references/screenshot-ipc.html)

The peer received zero of the expected 20 READY bytes before timeout. No supplied artifact captures the real `1 → 3 → 2 → 5` exchange, a type-2 framebuffer, or a successful correction. The publication therefore reports a **lifetime-hazard lead and a failed worker attempt**, while leaving successful deletion, a causal use-after-free diagnosis and a proven fix unresolved. A single build/environment record also cannot establish that PackClient screenshots universally fail. [Worker validation boundary](references/evidence.html)

sections.title: Tools, reproducibility and defensive use
sections.deck: The public tools decode Launcher and Core traffic, recover verified artifacts, and exercise the detections without executing malware.

blocks.text:
The repository ships two offline Python command-line tools and a phase-aware Wireshark Lua dissector. They decode Launcher and Core framing, distinguish the two type-`0x16` formats, label observed Core messages, validate `PV10`, and can export verified PLK1/Core and JPEG artifacts with a manifest tying each output to its source flow and frames. They do not execute samples, open sockets, resolve domains, or replay traffic. [Tooling](references/tooling.html)

The automated suite covers framing, handshake verification, both encryption formats, PLK1 reassembly and extraction, Core command parsing, `PV10`, capture reassembly, Wireshark integration, screenshot IPC, and detection-rule behavior. Historical captures were also used to recover the Core and extract the 15 observed JPEGs.

### Detection coverage

The Sigma rules cover the observed `NvSvc` task, anomalous 32-bit surrogate, screenshot-worker mode, and active-session mode. Suricata rules retain the plaintext markers already covered by Emerging Threats as regression checks and add stream-aware progression through PLK1, an observed Core startup response, and startup-to-`PV10` correlation. Separate compiled YARA rules identify the recovered Launcher and Core.

The Launcher rule matched all 86 retained Launcher mappings and none of 383 other retained objects. The Core rule matched the recovered DLL and all 352 retained Core mappings, with no matches among 116 Launcher/control allocations. Both rules also produced zero matches across more than 30,000 local Windows and installed-application PE files. The rules remain experimental because no representative enterprise-software or unrelated-malware corpus was tested. [Detection guide](references/detection-guide.html)

sections.title: Contribution and remaining questions
sections.deck: Recovered Launcher and Core implementation extend the public campaign account; plugin bytes and the external 1RCP peer remain unresolved.

blocks.text:
Proofpoint’s 27 August 2026 report is the public campaign anchor. It already describes the Tax Notice chain, modular Launcher/Core architecture, representative protocol markers and Emerging Threats coverage. Deception.Pro separately provides later PackClient hands-on-keyboard and ManageEngine context. This work adds the Launcher's recovered transport and loading contracts, direct Core reconstruction from PLK1 traffic, the signed-host/Donut/mapper chain, and the supporting detection and analysis tools. [Proofpoint campaign report](https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/carry-compromise-ta4922-packs-packclient), [Deception.Pro later reporting](https://blog.deception.pro/blog/new-packclient-hok-aug2026)

| Remaining gap | Evidence needed to close it | Present boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Plugin binaries | A preserved plugin transfer/cache/memory image with provenance | Loader and protocol exist; no plugin PE recovered |
| Carrier write primitive | Exact static write API/call site and installed instruction-pointer value | Runtime writes and primary-thread hijacking are established |
| External `1RCP` peer | Endpoint creation and type-2 consumption implementation | No confirmed bridge to Core `PV10` |
| Successful real `1RCP` exchange | Preserved READY/frame output tied to one controlled attempt | Static contract and synthetic agreement only |
| Deletion/crash causality | Captured deletion result and controlled attempt record | Lifetime hazard is not a proved cause or fix |
| Launcher envelope-key initialization | Writer and runtime values for the gated globals | Do not infer a PSK-to-key derivation |
| Server implementation | Server-side bytes/configuration | Historical captures prove behavior, not server code |
| September non-response cause | Server-side telemetry or controlled infrastructure | Inactive, gated and suppressed-response hypotheses remain open |
| Production detector accuracy | Representative malicious and benign corpora | No sensitivity/specificity claim |

Detailed Core behavior is documented in [PackClient Core](references/core-analysis.html). [Scope and limitations](references/limitations.html) records the remaining gaps.

status: Launcher-to-Core execution, delivery, persistence, and C2 behavior
abstract: This report follows PackClient from its signed-host carrier into a suspended 32-bit surrogate, the injected Donut package, Launcher execution, and a 985,088-byte Core recovered directly from historical PLK1 traffic. Reassembled sessions preserve successful authentication, Core delivery, plaintext commands, and 15 PV10 JPEG frames. The research also reconstructs the Core's plugin contracts, encryption, update storage, clipboard replacement, and screenshot producer, while keeping the unrecovered plugin binaries, external 1RCP peer, and server implementation explicit.
key_findings: A 985,088-byte PackClientCore.dll was recovered directly from historical PLK1 traffic; its .text matches all 352 retained Core memory mappings.
A complete PLH1 -> PLC1 -> PLA1 -> PLK1 session continues into bidirectional Core traffic and 15 PV10 JPEG frames.
Normal full-EXE execution persists the Tax Notice host, while direct carrier-DLL execution produces a broken rundll32.exe task without the original DLL argument.
